title: East & Southeast Asian Languages
summary: Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Indonesian and Thai: three unrelated families that shared a writing culture, plus tonal and non-tonal neighbours. Tone and script are the two thresholds for most English speakers.
sources: Li & Thompson: Mandarin Chinese: A Functional Reference Grammar
DeFrancis: The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy
Sneddon et al.: Indonesian: A Comprehensive Grammar

nodes.label: Mandarin: The Four Tones
nodes.summary: High, rising, dipping and falling tones distinguish words. Troublesome because English uses pitch for emotion, not meaning.
nodes.outcome: Hear and produce the four tones on minimal sets.
nodes.check: How many lexical tones does Standard Mandarin have, not counting the neutral tone?

nodes.label: Mandarin: Pinyin & Basics
nodes.summary: Pinyin romanisation, greetings and simple sentences.
nodes.outcome: Greet and introduce yourself in Mandarin.
nodes.check: How do you say 'hello' in Mandarin?

nodes.label: Chinese Characters & Radicals
nodes.summary: Characters built from components: a meaning radical plus, usually, a sound component.
nodes.outcome: Use radicals to guess meaning and look characters up.
nodes.check: What does the radical in a Chinese character usually tell you?
nodes.answer: Its meaning category (e.g. 氵 water), and it is used to look the character up.

nodes.label: "Chinese characters are pictures of things"
nodes.summary: Most characters are phono-semantic compounds that combine a meaning part with a sound part.
nodes.outcome: Split a phono-semantic character into its parts.
nodes.answer: No: most are phono-semantic compounds, combining a meaning component with a sound component.

nodes.label: Mandarin: Measure Words
nodes.summary: Numbers need a classifier before the noun: 一个人, 三本书.
nodes.check: Which measure word is most general in Mandarin, as in 一__人 (one person)?

nodes.label: Japanese: Hiragana, Katakana & Kanji
nodes.summary: Three scripts in one sentence: kanji for roots, hiragana for grammar, katakana for loanwords.
nodes.outcome: Read both kana syllabaries and identify each script in a sentence.
nodes.check: Which Japanese script is mainly used for foreign loanwords?

nodes.label: Japanese: Particles & SOV
nodes.summary: Particles after each phrase mark its role; the verb comes last.
nodes.outcome: Build sentences with は, が, を, に and で.
nodes.check: Which particle marks the direct object in Japanese?

nodes.label: Japanese: Basics & Politeness
nodes.summary: Polite (desu/masu) and plain speech; everyday phrases.
nodes.outcome: Greet and thank politely in Japanese.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' politely in Japanese?
nodes.answer: ありがとうございます (arigatō gozaimasu).

nodes.label: "Chinese, Japanese and Korean are closely related"
nodes.summary: They belong to different families; Japanese and Korean borrowed Chinese words and characters but have very different grammar.
nodes.check: Are Japanese and Korean related to Chinese the way Spanish is related to Italian?
nodes.answer: No: they are unrelated families; Japanese and Korean borrowed many Chinese words and characters but have very different (SOV, particle-based) grammar.

nodes.label: Korean: Hangul
nodes.summary: A featural alphabet whose letters are grouped into syllable blocks.
nodes.check: Who created Hangul, and roughly when?
nodes.answer: King Sejong the Great, in the 15th century (1443–1446).

nodes.label: Korean: Honorifics & Basics
nodes.summary: Speech levels and honorifics are built into the verb.
nodes.outcome: Choose a speech level and thank someone politely.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' politely in Korean?

nodes.label: Vietnamese: Tones in a Latin Script
nodes.summary: Tone marks on the Latin alphabet; an isolating grammar with no inflection.
nodes.outcome: Read tone marks and greet in Vietnamese.
nodes.check: How many tones does Northern (Hanoi) Vietnamese have?

nodes.label: Indonesian
nodes.summary: No tones or verb conjugation; meaning built with affixes and reduplication.
nodes.outcome: Form plurals and derived verbs in Indonesian.
nodes.check: How do you make 'anak' (child) plural in Indonesian?

nodes.label: Thai: Script & Tones
nodes.summary: An abugida with five tones and no spaces between words.
nodes.outcome: Read Thai tone markers and segment a sentence.
nodes.check: Does written Thai put spaces between words?
nodes.answer: No: spaces mark the ends of phrases or sentences, not individual words.
